clue.text: Extremely debatable — intended to make a challenge

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the following word, its first and last letters only

parts.note: the two end letters of the word
one's intended is the person one is engaged to marry

explanation.surface: Someone means a deliberately contentious remark as a provocation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intended' reads as a verb (meant), but it is the noun for a betrothed partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Defiance is open resistance, a bold refusal that throws down a challenge to authority.

clue.text: Told stories recalled about volunteers, soldiers given a special task

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the turned word goes round the volunteers
recalled suggests calling back, so the word for telling stories runs back up the entry

parts.note: told stories means told untruths
the TA, Territorial Army, was Britain's volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: Someone recounts tales of volunteer soldiers sent on a special mission.
explanation.walkthrough: The TA (Territorial Army) is the crossword's usual volunteers; the clue's soldiers belong to the definition, not the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A detail is a small group of soldiers assigned to a particular duty, a military usage.

clue.text: Society member, independent male when working

parts.note: free means independent, not controlled by others
M is the abbreviation for male
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
on means working, as a machine that is switched on

explanation.surface: A self-employed man joins a club for when he is at work.
explanation.walkthrough: The masons' fraternity calls itself a society, which makes the opening words a fair definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A freemason belongs to the fraternal order of Free and Accepted Masons, a secretive society.

clue.text: Further loan

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a verb, to promote or help forward
second meaning: money paid out ahead of time

explanation.walkthrough: Further reads as an adjective (another loan), but it is a verb meaning to promote.
explanation.definitionFit: To advance a cause is to further it, and an advance is money lent or paid early.

clue.text: Job centre — husband must go in

indicators.note: going in means being placed inside the other word

parts.note: the core is the centre of something
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: At the employment office a husband is told he must go in to find work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Job centre' is the British name for a government employment office, but here the two words split into the definition and a piece of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A chore is a routine task, especially a domestic one such as washing up, so a job.

clue.text: A year inside squat obtaining sanctuary

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: inside tells you the year sits within the word for squat

parts.note: a squat is a run-down dwelling, a slum
Y is the standard abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A squatter spends a year in an occupied building and finds refuge there.
explanation.walkthrough: Squat looks like a verb or adjective, but here it is the noun for squalid housing.
explanation.definitionFit: Asylum is protection or refuge granted to someone fleeing danger, the same idea as sanctuary.

clue.text: Knife left in various places

indicators.note: in places the side letter inside the rearranged word
various suggests a medley of arrangements, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A knife has been left lying about all over the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left in various places' reads as scattered, but various shuffles places and L goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A scalpel is the small, very sharp knife a surgeon uses.

clue.text: Knight having no chance to find weapon

indicators.note: having no means going without, so the word for chance is taken out

parts.note: Sir Lancelot, the Arthurian knight
a lot is something decided by chance, as in drawing lots

explanation.surface: An unlucky knight goes in search of arms.
explanation.walkthrough: Knight is usually K or N in crosswords; here it is a whole famous knight of the Round Table.
explanation.definitionFit: A lance is a long spear carried by a mounted knight, so a weapon.

clue.text: Grow rapidly in Greek character's hot apartment

parts.note: mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet, plus the 's
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
a room is one apartment of a house

explanation.surface: Something flourishes in a Greek man's overheated flat.
explanation.walkthrough: Greek character looks like a person, but it is a letter of the Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: To mushroom is to expand fast, as the fungi spring up overnight.

clue.text: Mysterious man, holding up boozer, is after key

indicators.note: in a down entry, holding something up means sitting beneath it, so the drinker goes on top
after puts everything else behind the musical key, which comes first

parts.note: E is a musical key
a sot is a habitual drunkard
a man's name

explanation.surface: A shadowy figure holds up a pub in search of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Boozer is British slang for both a pub and a drinker; here it is the drinker. Holding up suggests a robbery, but it places the man below the drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoteric means understood only by an inner few, hence obscure or mysterious.

clue.text: Poem about Cornish resort village, written by the girl

parts.note: surface reading: a poem describing a seaside village in Cornwall, which happens to share its name with a saint
setter's reading: the title can be read as naming a girl from that village as its author, a first woman's name plus her home

explanation.surface: A local girl writes verses about her Cornish seaside village.
explanation.walkthrough: THE EVE OF ST AGNES is Keats's poem; St Agnes is also a resort village on the north Cornish coast, so the title reads as 'the Eve from St Agnes', a girl credited as its author.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats wrote this narrative poem in 1819 about the superstition attached to the night before Saint Agnes's feast day.

clue.text: Huge mines exploded around me

indicators.note: around says the rearranged letters wrap themselves about the word me
something exploded is blown apart, so the letters of mines are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier describes enormous explosions going off all about him.
explanation.walkthrough: Mines rearranges to IMNSE, and ME goes in after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Immense means extremely large, a straightforward synonym for huge.

clue.text: Best clobber — one may drive in it

parts.note: top means best, as in top marks
clobber is British slang for clothes or kit, also called gear

explanation.surface: Someone puts on their finest outfit, fit for a smart drive out.
explanation.walkthrough: Clobber looks like a verb meaning to hit, but it is the British noun for clothing. TOP GEAR is the highest gear of a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's highest gear is the one a motorist cruises along in at speed, so one may drive in it.

clue.text: Idiots to be brought before sheriff, initially, or judge

indicators.note: brought before places the fools at the front, ahead of the official who follows

parts.note: asses are fools

indicators.note: initially asks for just the opening letter of the word it follows

parts.note: the first letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fools are hauled up in front of a sheriff or a magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a courtroom, so 'judge' looks like more of the scene, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessor evaluates or appraises, and in law sits as an adviser helping to decide a case, so a judge.

clue.text: Avoid team that has upset favourites

parts.note: a side is a sports team

indicators.note: upset means turned upside down, so in a down entry the word reads from the bottom

parts.note: pets are favourites, as teacher's pets

explanation.surface: Steer clear of a team that has knocked out the favourites.
explanation.walkthrough: Upset sounds like a sporting shock, but it turns the favourites word round.
explanation.definitionFit: To sidestep a problem is to dodge it, as a player steps aside from a tackle.

clue.text: Game, extremely tight after opener's dismissed

indicators.note: the opener is the first in line, and once dismissed it leaves the word

parts.note: tight means drunk, and very drunk is slang blotto

explanation.surface: A cricket match grows tense once the opening batsman is out.
explanation.walkthrough: Opener and dismissed are cricket words, but here they only drop the B. Lotto is a game of chance like bingo, also a name for lotteries.
explanation.definitionFit: Lotto is a game in which players mark numbers drawn at random, much like bingo.

clue.text: Land feeling depressed

parts.note: touch is the sense of feeling
down means low in spirits

explanation.surface: A country that feels gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: Land looks like a noun (country), but it is a verb, as an aircraft lands.
explanation.definitionFit: To touch down is to come in to land, said of an aircraft or spacecraft.

clue.text: Char holding top of soft detergent

indicators.note: holding means the first word grips the other inside it

parts.note: a char, short for charwoman, is a British cleaning lady

indicators.note: in a down entry the top of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady clutches a bottle of gentle washing liquid.
explanation.walkthrough: Char looks like burn, but it is the British word for a woman paid to clean houses.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleanser is a cleaning agent, and detergent is one such substance.

clue.text: Joins golf course

definitions.meaning: first meaning: connects or ties together
second meaning: a seaside course among dunes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as someone becoming a golf club member; the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means connects; as a noun it is a golf course, especially on coastal sandy ground.

clue.text: Swank cabaret cancelled

parts.note: a cabaret is a nightclub show
an event that is off has been cancelled

explanation.surface: A posh nightclub act is called off.
explanation.walkthrough: Swank reads as an adjective (posh), but it is a verb meaning to flaunt.
explanation.definitionFit: To swank is to boast or flaunt oneself, which is to parade one's assets ostentatiously.

clue.text: An easy task in dense fog? There's nothing to it!

parts.words: An easy task in dense fog?
parts.note: surface reading: a simple job that gets done even when visibility is poor
setter's reading: the cricket word for a score of zero sits inside a word for thick fog, and an easy task is one with nothing to it

explanation.surface: Someone claims a job in thick fog is no trouble at all.
explanation.walkthrough: DUCK SOUP is slang for something easily done. A duck is a cricket score of nothing, and soup (pea-souper) is a dense fog, so fog with nothing in it is this very phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Duck soup is American slang for a task so simple it needs no effort, a cinch.

clue.text: Mishandle wages completely

parts.note: screw is old British slang for wages or salary
up can mean completely, as in eat up or use up

explanation.surface: Someone bungles the whole payroll.
explanation.walkthrough: Screw for pay is dated British slang, as in 'a good screw'.
explanation.definitionFit: To screw up is a colloquial way to make a mess of something through bad handling.

clue.text: Note villain's accent

parts.note: B is a musical note
a rogue is a scoundrel

explanation.surface: Pay attention to how the baddie speaks.
explanation.walkthrough: Note reads as a verb (observe), but it is a musical note.
explanation.definitionFit: A brogue is a strong regional accent, especially an Irish or Scottish one.

clue.text: Uncertain what to do, with income less than outlay?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: baffled, not knowing how to act
second meaning: trading so that money taken in falls short of money spent

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second meaning as a literal, business reading of an idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means bewildered, while a firm trading this way is spending more than it earns.

clue.text: A well-bred fellow envoy

parts.note: taken as written
a gent, short for gentleman, is a man of good breeding

explanation.surface: A refined gentleman serves as a diplomat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow envoy' reads as a colleague, but fellow belongs with well-bred.
explanation.definitionFit: An agent acts on behalf of another, as an envoy represents a government abroad.

clue.text: Put horse through awfully cruel run — a hunting animal

indicators.note: putting one thing through another runs it into the middle of it
awfully suggests something done badly, so the letters of the cruel word are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A horse is driven through a brutal course in a hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: Horse is drug slang for heroin, written H. A LURCHER is a crossbred dog, often greyhound and collie, used for coursing hares and poaching.
explanation.definitionFit: The lurcher is a fast crossbred dog traditionally kept for hunting rabbits and hares.

clue.text: Learning about one in department

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for learning surrounds the one

parts.note: lore is traditional knowledge or learning
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Studying a single subject within a university department.
explanation.walkthrough: Department suggests an office, but it means one of France's administrative areas, named after the river.
explanation.definitionFit: Loire is a French département, one of the regions France is divided into for government.

clue.text: Cast, home-grown, in new movie

parts.note: to cast off a skin or coat is to shed it

indicators.note: new signals the preceding letters are made into something fresh, a rearrangement

parts.note: the letters of these words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A new film boasts an all-local cast of actors.
explanation.walkthrough: Cast looks like the actors, but it is a verb meaning shed. SHE DONE HIM WRONG is the 1933 Mae West film.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of a 1933 Hollywood comedy starring Mae West and Cary Grant, so a movie.

clue.text: Sign, please, in leader's absence

indicators.note: with the leader absent, the first letter of the word is missing

parts.note: to please someone is to gratify them

explanation.surface: A request to put a signature on something while the boss is away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign, please' sounds like a polite request; Sign is the definition and please is the word to trim.
explanation.definitionFit: To ratify a treaty or agreement is to give it formal approval, typically by signing it.

clue.text: Displaced persons, last to receive an answer

indicators.note: displaced means moved out of place, so these letters are shuffled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

indicators.note: last asks only for the final letter of the following word

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Refugees are the last people to get a reply to their applications.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Displaced persons' looks like a fixed phrase for refugees, but it splits into an indicator and its fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A response is a reply, something said or written in answer to a question.
